facts.statement: Listracanthus lived from the Late Carboniferous to the Early Triassic.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Carboniferous to Early Triassic

facts.statement: The genus Listracanthus was described by Newberry and Worthen in 1870.
Known species of Listracanthus include L. beyrichi, L. eliasi, L. hildrethi, L. hystrix, L. pectenatus, L. wardi, and L. woltersi.
facts.quote: subdivision: *L. beyrichi von Koenen, 1879 L. eliasi Hibbard, 1938 L. hildrethi Newberry, 1875 L. hystrix Newberry & Worthen, 1870 (type) L. pectenatus Mutter & Neuman, 2006 L. wardi Woodward, 1891 L. woltersi Schmidt, 1949

facts.statement: Listracanthus is known primarily from its tremendous, feather-like denticles that can reach up to four inches in length.
facts.quote: Species of Listracanthus are known primarily from their tremendous, feather-like denticles, which range up to four inches in length.

facts.statement: The denticles of Listracanthus featured a large main spine with secondary spines radiating from the sides like feather barbs or a comb.
facts.quote: The denticles had a large main spine, from which secondary spines emanate from the sides, like the barbs of a feather or a comb.

facts.statement: Listracanthus first appeared in Late Carboniferous strata in North America and disappeared from the fossil record during the Early Triassic.
facts.quote: Listracanthus first appeared in late Carboniferous strata in North America, and eventually disappear from the fossil record some time during the Early Triassic.

facts.statement: Some authors suggest Listracanthus may be a member of Menaspiformes because denticles similar to those of Listracanthus have been found with remains of that group, despite the lack of eel-like bodies in those fossils.
facts.quote: other authors have noted that Listracanthus-like denticles have been found associated with the remains of Menaspiformes like Deltoptychius (which do not have eel-like bodies), and have suggested that Listracanthus is a member of this group.

facts.statement: Listracanthus appeared in Late Carboniferous strata in North America and disappeared during the Upper Triassic, making it one of the longest-lived genera in the family Edestidae.
facts.quote: Listracanthus apareció por primera vez en los estratos a finales del Carbonífero en América del Norte, y eventualmente desapareció del registro fósil algún momento durante el Triásico Superior, por lo que es uno de los géneros con vida más largos en la familia Edestidae.

facts.statement: The main denticles of Listracanthus were located on the vertebral column, with secondary spines emanating from the skin like a feather or a comb.
facts.quote: Los dentículos principales se encontraban en la columna vertebral, con espinas secundarias que emanaban de la piel, como una pluma o un peine.

facts.statement: Based on Zangerl's account, Ray Troll reconstructed Listracanthus as resembling a shark with feathers.
facts.quote: el Listracanthus reconstruido se asemejaría a un tiburón con plumas.

facts.statement: Listracanthus is classified within the family Edestidae.
The authority for the genus Listracanthus is Newberry & Worthen, 1870.
Species of Listracanthus include L. beyrichi, L. eliasi, L. hildrethi, L. hystrix, L. pectenatus, L. spinatus, L. wardi, and L. woltersi.
facts.quote: subdivision: L. beyrichi L. eliasi L. hildrethi L. hystrix L. pectenatus L. spinatus L. wardi L. woltersi

facts.statement: The type species of the genus Listracanthus is Listracanthus hystrix.
There are 22 recorded fossil occurrences of the genus Listracanthus in the Paleobiology Database.

rejected.quote: They also erected the family Listracanthidae to encompass the two genera.
